newsitem.title: FRANCE: France withholds support from U.S. raid on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: France withholds support from U.S. raid on Iraq.

text.p: France, one of the Gulf War allies, withheld support for a U.S. cruise missile attack on Iraq on Tuesday while urging Baghdad to withdraw its forces from Kurdish areas of northern Iraq.
A Foreign Ministry statement said France had been "informed in advance of the operation conducted this morning by the United States" but pointedly avoided any backing for the raid.

French officials said President Bill Clinton telephoned President Jacques Chirac on Monday night to inform him of the impending 27-missile blitz on military targets in southern Iraq in retaliation for an offensive by President Saddam Hussein's troops against Kurdish areas of northern Iraq.
Chirac made clear he understood Clinton's motives, in the midst of the U.S. presidential election campaign, but differed on the appropriateness of military action, the officials said.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry called the exchange "a useful, productive and candid discussion", suggesting there was some disagreement.
Implicitly challenging the legality of the U.S. raid, French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said Paris did not believe the Iraqi offensive violated U.N. resolutions.

"We do not see that United Nations resolutions are called into question by the Iraqi intervention, especially since there was a written request by one of the main Kurdish movements. Iraq is acting entirely on its own soil," he told reporters.

The Iraqi government says the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) asked for military support against the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which it accused of having military backing from neighbouring Iran.
Paris fought alongside the United States in the Gulf War to drive Iraqi invasion forces out of Kuwait in 1991 and is one of the allies enforcing no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq.
But as Iraq's biggest creditor and erstwhile arms supplier, it is keen to ease the U.N. economic embargo against Iraq.

"France expresses its concern at the development of the situation in Iraq," the Foreign Ministry statement said. "In a message sent last night by (Foreign Minister) Herve de Charette to Iraqi Vice-Prime Minister Tareq Aziz, France stressed the need to continue withdrawing effectively the forces involved on the ground, as the Iraqi authorities had announced on Sunday."

De Charette emphasized the international community's concern for the safety of the civilian population and said only a dialogue between Baghdad and the Kurdish factions could lead to the restoration of stability through a political settlement.
Rummelhardt said France had given no instruction to its nationals to leave Iraq and said he hoped a United Nations-brokered oil-for-food pact would soon be implemented.
The United Nations said on Sunday it was delaying the plan's implementation to assure the safety of its staff.
French officials said Clinton had not asked U.S. allies to join in the military strike and Chirac had not sought actively to dissuade him.

They said the strike should be seen in the context of the U.S. presidential campaign. Clinton's Republican challenger Bob Dole had accused the Democratic president of weakness in his response to the Iraqi offensive.
The officials said that while Paris differed with Washington on the raid, Chirac would not publicly criticise Clinton, who is hot favourite to win re-election in November.
